name: Fatima Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Fatima, thanks for talking with me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will be traced back to you. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm 27, and I'm a marketing specialist at Crumb & Co, a plant-based crisp and snack brand, at their office on the business park outside town. My mornings are the social media calendar: what we post, which influencers we send boxes to, how the comments are going. Afternoons are in-store promotions, like the two-for-one deals and the shelf signs for the big supermarkets.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good bit is the team. Jonah and I sit together and we make each other laugh through the boring parts, and Harriet, our boss, actually listens. The hard bit is money: I'm paid on the low side, I share a flat with my friend Ines, and I've got less than a month's rent put by. There aren't many jobs like mine round here, so I can't just hop to another brand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll ask a chatbot for ten caption ideas when my brain is empty at four o'clock, then I rewrite the best two. I waited until Jonah had used it for a few months before I tried it myself, which is pretty typical of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so it stays as a caption helper. That's more or less where it is now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently, to the people who said it would replace us all. Online I'd share something about how human creativity still matters. At work I'd probably just get on with the next campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's probably fine in that world, but my money isn't. Prices keep going up, my pay doesn't, and one broken laptop would wipe out my savings. The AI part was never really the thing keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, using the chatbot for ideas now and then. I'd set up a standing order of forty a month into savings the day I get paid, so it's gone before I can spend it. And I'd ask Harriet about a pay review in the spring, with my campaign numbers in hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit tired, like the news cycle wore me out over nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a broken laptop would wipe you out. Has something like that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter my phone screen cracked and it took me two months to stop feeling the hole in my account. Ines lent me the money for the repair, and I hated asking. That's how close to the edge it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in front of Harriet at that pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The summer promotion with the big supermarket, where our crisp sales went up by a fifth. I planned every shelf sign for that one. If that doesn't earn a raise, I don't know what does.

say: I'd say, gently, that **human creativity** still matters in marketing.
At work I'd **get on** with the next campaign and not gloat.
think: I think my **job is fine**, but my money isn't.
Rising prices and **flat pay** worry me more than AI ever did.
do: Keep using the chatbot only for **caption ideas** when stuck.
Set up a **standing order** of forty a month into savings.
Ask Harriet for a **pay review** in spring, with campaign numbers.
feel: I feel **mostly okay**, just **tired** from all the noise about AI.
S0.quote: Last winter my phone screen cracked and it took me two months to stop feeling the hole in my account.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **money**, not technology: low pay and under a month saved.
She has a **concrete case** for a raise and plans to use it.
Asking her friend for a loan left a mark; **pride** matters to her.

steps.text: Use the chatbot only for caption ideas on slow afternoons
Set up a forty-a-month standing order on payday
Bring the summer promotion results to a spring pay review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, planning, answering customers. That's most of my week, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say companies need rules about this: tell staff what's coming, and don't just stop hiring quietly. I'd post about it and probably share union stuff. With Jonah I'd be more blunt and say we need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Crumb & Co stops replacing people. If Jonah or I left, nobody would come in, and the one who stays would do two jobs with AI. I'd be fine for a year or so, but the job I'd have in three years is not the job I have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the AI course the company offers, once I'd seen it actually help Jonah with something real. I'd get the two of us and the design team to ask Harriet for a written promise about training before any cuts. I'd keep the forty a month going and try to push it to sixty. I'd also look at what the union for office and creative workers charges to join.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of fight in it. I don't like being the last to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see it help Jonah. Why not just go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people jump on every shiny thing and waste weeks. I'm not against it, I just want proof. Jonah's the one who tries things; I'm the one who asks if they worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it cost you to push savings to sixty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Friday drinks, mostly, and the online shopping I do when I'm stressed. Ines would notice I'm in more. She'd probably be glad of the company.

say: I'd say firms need **clear rules**: tell staff, and don't stop hiring quietly.
I'd tell Jonah we need to **look after each other** at work.
think: I think Crumb & Co will **stop replacing people** who leave.
In three years my **job will change** into two jobs done with AI.
do: Take the **company AI course** once it's proven to help Jonah.
Ask Harriet, with the team, for a **written promise** on training.
Raise savings from forty to **sixty a month** by cutting Friday drinks.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with a bit of **fight** in it.
S1.quote: The job I'd have in three years is not the job I have now.
fieldNote: She expects **quiet shrinking**, not sudden layoffs, and plans for it.
She'll learn the tools, but only after **proof** from a colleague.
Her first instinct is **collective**: get the team to ask together.

steps.text: Take the Crumb & Co AI course after seeing Jonah use it
Ask Harriet with the team for a written promise on training
Push savings to sixty a month by dropping Friday drinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's before my student loan is even half paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be handled by government, fast: income support, retraining paid for, rules on mass layoffs. I'd go to a rally if there was one. I'd also say it to anyone at work who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my whole job goes by 2028. A snack brand doesn't need a person to plan posts when the AI can plan them, write them and answer the comments. The robots only come around 2031, so the jobs that last a few years more are the ones where you use your hands or look after people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying straight away for hands-on or care work, maybe as a care assistant, because people will still want a human there for a few years. I'd cut everything that isn't rent and food. I'd write to my local representative, and I'd find out exactly what support I could claim before I needed it, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I keep doing the sums in my head and they don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Care work is a big change. What makes you think of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum was a care assistant for years, and she always said they were short of people. It's hard, and the pay's low, but it's pay. And it's work with your hands and your heart, which the thinking AI can't do on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first, the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines, because she'd be losing her flatmate's rent if I lost my job. Then my mum. I'd ask her what the first day of care work is really like.

say: I'd demand **income support**, paid retraining and rules on mass layoffs.
I'd go to a **rally** and talk about it at work.
think: I think my **whole job goes** by 2028.
Work with **hands or care** lasts a few years longer, until robots around 2031.
do: Apply for **care assistant** jobs straight away, like my mum did.
Find out what **support** I could claim and write to my representative.
feel: I feel **frightened**; the **sums don't work** in my head.
S2.quote: A snack brand doesn't need a person to plan posts when the AI can plan them, write them and answer the comments.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** by 2028 and has no cushion.
Her fallback is **care work**, learned from her mother's life.
Even in a crisis, she thinks first of how her loss would hit her **flatmate**.

steps.text: Apply for care assistant jobs at local care homes
Cut spending to rent and food only
Check which job-loss benefits she could claim, before she needs them
Write to her local representative asking for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a bit different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's use it: retraining money now, not a rescue later. I'd sign the petitions and say it at work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job still goes around 2031. But I'd have time to watch what happens to the first jobs that get hit, and then move once I can see what's actually working for people. That suits me better than jumping blind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give it a year, keep my job, and keep saving the sixty. I'd watch which retraining routes people like me actually get jobs from. Then, by the second year, I'd start a part-time course, probably in nursing support, since care work has a few extra years before the robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steadier. Like I can see the cliff, and there's a path down it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said give it a year. What if the year slips into three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the danger with me, honestly. I'd put a date on the fridge: if I haven't started a course by the January after next, I start one anyway. Ines would hold me to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about Crumb & Co?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, and the silly days, like when we dressed up as crisps for the shop launch. I'd also miss being good at something. Starting again at 29 means being bad at something for a while.

say: I'd say use the time for **retraining money** now, not a rescue later.
I'd sign **petitions** and raise it at work.
think: I think my job **still goes** around 2031.
Five years lets me **watch first** and move once I see what works.
do: Stay at Crumb & Co for **one year** and keep saving sixty a month.
Start a **part-time nursing support** course by the second year.
Put a **deadline on the fridge** so waiting doesn't drag on.
feel: I feel **uneasy but steadier**, like there's a **path** down the cliff.
S3.quote: Starting again at 29 means being bad at something for a while.
fieldNote: Her steady nature fits a **watch, then move** plan, and she knows its risk.
She sets a **hard deadline** to stop herself waiting too long.
Losing **mastery** of her craft hurts as much as losing the pay.

steps.text: Stay at Crumb & Co for one year and watch retraining routes
Keep saving sixty a month into the standing order
Start a part-time nursing support course by the second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That feels almost manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to do it right: laws, training and a safety net before 2036. I'd volunteer for a campaign group, maybe, if there was a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd still have to leave marketing. But ten years is long enough to train properly, even work part-time in care while I study. I wouldn't have to panic, I'd just have to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Crumb & Co for a few years and learn the AI tools well, because they'd keep me useful meanwhile. Around year three I'd start a nursing degree part-time. I'd keep saving, and I'd vote for whoever puts real money into retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, a bit. Also a bit sad, because I picked marketing on purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made you pick marketing in the first place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I loved adverts as a kid; I used to rewrite the cereal box slogans. It felt like a job where you could be clever for a living. Turns out a computer can be clever for a living too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably put off moving out of the shared flat. A place of my own was the plan for next year, but I'd rather keep the rent low and pay for a course.

say: I'd say a decade is time to set up **laws** and a **safety net**.
I'd **volunteer** with a good campaign group if there was one.
think: I think I'd **still leave marketing** in the end.
Ten years lets me **train properly**, even working part-time in care, without panic.
do: Learn the **AI tools** well to stay useful for a few years.
Start a **part-time nursing degree** around year three.
Put off **moving out** to keep rent low for course fees.
feel: I feel a little **hopeful**, and a little **sad** to leave a job I chose.
S4.quote: I loved adverts as a kid; I used to rewrite the cereal box slogans.
fieldNote: The long warning lets her plan a **proper career change** into nursing.
She'd use **AI tools** to stay useful while she studies.
She'd delay a **flat of her own** to fund the move.

steps.text: Learn the company AI tools well over the next two years
Start a part-time nursing degree around year three
Put off moving out of the shared flat to fund studies
Vote for parties that fund retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no savings. What would help is a proper income for a year while I retrain, and a course that leads to a real job, not just a certificate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who people like me talk to. Most of my friends are in the same boat: young, renting, nothing saved. Nobody's parents can bail everyone out.

headlineQuote: Turns out a computer can be clever for a living too.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old campaign planner** at a plant-based snack brand, sharing a flat and saving little.
She uses AI **now and then** and waits for proof before changing how she works.
She leans left and wants **rules, unions** and public retraining money.
She moves from **uneasy** about money to **alarmed** when AGI comes in two years.
With time, she would **retrain in nursing**, following her mother into care.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she would have no time and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **year of income** while she retrains.
A course that leads to a **real job**, not just a certificate.
